final_answer: Corporate tax cuts rarely boost long-term employment because they primarily benefit shareholders through stock buybacks and dividends rather than wage growth or hiring. Empirical studies of major corporate tax reforms show little to no persistent effect on employment levels. Businesses invest based on consumer demand, technology, labor costs, and regulatory environment—not marginal tax rate changes. When corporations do pass savings to workers, the effect is modest and temporary. Meanwhile, cutting corporate taxes without offsetting spending reductions increases deficits, which can crowd out public investment in infrastructure, education, and R&D that actually drive job creation. Most economists agree that targeted policies—skills training, R&D credit expansion, streamlined regulation—create more durable employment gains than broad corporate tax reductions. The trickle-down narrative lacks robust support from economic data across multiple countries and time periods.
